title: Efficacy of Levetiracetam Combined with Sodium Valproate (Oral) in the Treatment of Senile Epilepsy and Its Effects on Cognitive Function, Inflammatory Factors and Neurotransmitters.
abstract:
To evaluate the clinical efficacy of levetiracetam combined with oral sodium valproate in elderly patients with epilepsy and to assess its effects on cognitive function, inflammatory markers, and neurotransmitter levels.
Seventy elderly patients with epilepsy treated between January and December 2021 were randomly assigned to a study group receiving levetiracetam plus sodium valproate or a control group receiving sodium valproate alone, with 35 patients in each group. Seizure frequency and duration, cognitive function assessed by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, serum inflammatory factors including tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin six, neurotransmitters including serotonin and dopamine, and overall clinical efficacy were compared between groups after treatment.
Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were comparable between the two groups. After treatment, seizure frequency and seizure duration were significantly reduced in the combination therapy group compared with the control group. Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores were significantly higher in the combination group. Serum tumor necrosis factor alpha and interleukin six levels were significantly decreased, while serotonin and dopamine levels were significantly increased in the study group. The total clinical effective rate in the combination therapy group was significantly higher than that in the control group, and all differences reached statistical significance.
Levetiracetam combined with sodium valproate demonstrated superior comprehensive efficacy in the treatment of senile epilepsy. This regimen effectively improved seizure control, cognitive function, inflammatory status, and neurotransmitter balance, supporting its value as a reliable therapeutic option for elderly patients with epilepsy under routine clinical conditions and standardized hospital treatment protocols.

title: Neuroprotective effects of lithium and caffeic acid co-loaded liposomes in diabetes-induced Alzheimer's disease: association with GSK-3β and β-catenin.
abstract:
To investigate the therapeutic effects of co-loaded lithium (Li) and caffeic acid (CA) liposomes in diabetes-induced Alzheimer's disease rats by improving cognitive dysfunction and attenuating neurodegeneration through the modulation of β-catenin/GSK-3β signaling.
Li- and CA-co-loaded liposomes were prepared by the ethanol injection method and characterized. A diabetes-induced Alzheimer's disease model was established in male Wistar rats using a high-fat diet followed by low-dose streptozotocin (35 mg/kg) administered intraperitoneally. Li- and CA-co-loaded liposomes were given via the same route every day for 4 weeks. At the end of the experiment, the animals were sacrificed, and various biochemical and oxidative stress parameters, histopathological assessments, and ELISA analyses were performed.
Dual-drug-loaded Li and CA liposomal treatment significantly improved cognitive function, ameliorated metabolic dysfunction, and reduced oxidative stress by restoring antioxidant enzyme levels. Additionally, liposomes attenuated nitrite, acetylcholinesterase, and amyloid-β levels in diabetes-induced Alzheimer's rats. Histopathological assessment confirmed marked neuroprotective and pancreatic protective effects. Further, at a molecular level, Li and CA liposomal treatment reduced the expression of GSK-3β and increased the expression of β-catenin levels in rats.
This study provides the first evidence demonstrating the therapeutic potential of Li- and CA-co-loaded liposomes in attenuating diabetes‑associated cognitive dysfunction.

title: Nose-to-brain delivery of a novel boronated curcuminoid via cyclodextrins: Biodistribution toward potential BNCT applications in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: This study investigates the selective accumulation of a boronated monocarbonyl curcuminoid (BMAC-9) complexed with β-cyclodextrins in the amyloid-rich brain regions of APP/PS1dE9 transgenic mice, an established model of Alzheimer's disease, compared to C57BL/6 healthy mice. The goal is to develop and evaluate a novel delivery system for the boronated curcuminoid BMAC-9 and to determine whether the resulting boron concentrations in the brain, particularly in the cortex and hippocampus, which are typically enriched in amyloid plaques in patients with Alzheimer's disease, could reach levels potentially suitable for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT). Physicochemical characterization displayed that BMAC-9 has a logD of 3.45 at both physiological (7.4) and nasal (5.5) pH, suggesting good membrane permeability but poor aqueous solubility. To optimize delivery and facilitate blood-brain barrier (BBB) crossing, inclusion complexes were formulated using hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HP-β-CD) and a cationic cyclodextrin polymer (TMA-poly-β-CD). These systems, exhibiting stability constants in the 103-105 M-1 range, significantly enhanced drug solubility. In vitro assays on SH-SY5Y cells demonstrated low cytotoxicity at short incubation times confirming that drug release and cellular uptake depend on CD binding affinity. In vivo biodistribution analysis through boron quantification by ICP-MS in C57BL/6 mice exhibit that intranasal administration achieves effective brain targeting while reducing systemic exposure compared to the intravenous one. Interestingly, the BMAC-9/HP-β-CD complex showed selective accumulation in Aβ plaque-rich brain areas only in APP/PS1dE9 transgenic mice. This selectivity is crucial for BNCT efficacy and offers a promising solution to the persistent challenge of targeted drug delivery in neurodegenerative diseases.

title: The Advanced Therapeutics for Alzheimer's Disease Review Board: A multidisciplinary model to facilitate safe access to amyloid-targeting therapies in general neurology across the Sutter Health system.
abstract: Amyloid-targeting therapies (ATTs) require workup and monitoring that some general neurologists are uncomfortable with. Sutter Health treats over 3.5 million patients with more than 100 neurologists, but only 5 cognitive specialists. We developed the Advanced Therapeutics for Alzheimer's Disease (ATAD) Review Board, a system-wide model to address the shortage of specialists while enhancing safe access to ATTs across the health system. The ATAD Review Board comprises cognitive specialists, a neuroradiologist, a pharmacist, and a registered nurse program manager. Neurologists submit cases to the board for appropriate patient selection and re-review of cases with side effects. We reviewed 447 cases from 51 neurologists and 77% were eligible for treatment. The annual volume increased 148% in 2025. Total amyloid-related imaging abnormality rate was 17.4% for lecanemab and 28.8% for donanemab. We describe a system-wide review board model that supported ATT prescribing by general neurologists and expanded safe access to ATTs across a large integrated health system.

title: DeMorph: A Decoupled Deformation Model with Anatomical Guidance for Predicting Longitudinal Brain Atrophy.
abstract: Modeling the longitudinal progression of brain atrophy in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is critical for early diagnosis and prognosis, but remains challenging for existing generative models. Current methods either fail to preserve anatomical integrity or treat progression as an entangled process, where changes from normal aging are inseparably fused with AD pathology. This fundamentally limits their scientific utility. To address this, we propose DeMorph, a novel deformation-based framework that explicitly disentangles and accurately predicts longitudinal brain MRI changes. Our transformer-based architecture features two key innovations: (1) a Decoupled Feed-Forward Network (D-FFN) for separate aging and pathology deformation pathways; and (2) a Multi-Scale Anatomical Guidance Cross-Attention (MS-AGCA) module, which explicitly injects anatomical priors to ensure spatially precise and biologically plausible disentanglement. Extensive experiments on four datasets (ADNI, OASIS-3, AIBL, and an inhouse dataset) demonstrate that DeMorph achieves stateof- the-art performance in both image similarity and anatomical accuracy. Crucially, we validate the success of our framework through robust bidirectional counterfactual synthesis, demonstrating the ability to controllably induce and remove a quantitatively plausible, AD-specific pathological effect.

title: Valproate use in low- and middle-income countries: Balancing reproductive safety, seizure control, and access to safer antiseizure medicines.
abstract: Valproate is highly effective for genetic generalized epilepsies but carries substantial dose-dependent risks of major congenital malformations and adverse neurodevelopment after in utero exposure. Guidelines therefore recommend avoiding it in individuals with pregnancy potential when effective alternatives are available. This dilemma is concentrated in generalized epilepsies; focal epilepsies should generally be treated with other appropriate antiseizure medicines irrespective of reproductive potential. In many low- and middle-income countries, however, inconsistent access to lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and ethosuximide, limited specialist and reproductive-health services, and weak procurement and pharmacovigilance constrain substitution. This narrative review integrates comparative efficacy, pregnancy-safety, health-economic, and implementation evidence. We distinguish cost-effectiveness from short-term budget impact and argue that restriction without reliable alternative supply may worsen seizure control and inequity. We propose syndrome-specific prescribing: prioritise safer alternatives, reserve valproate for documented cases in which they are ineffective, contraindicated, unavailable, or unaffordable, and pair its use with counselling, effective contraception, folic acid, lowest-effective-dose monotherapy, and regular review. National policies should combine reproductive safeguards with essentialmedicines inclusion, pooled procurement, quality assurance, and monitoring.

title: Integrating network medicine and foundation models reveals cell-type-specific regulatory alterations in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease is a complex neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline and neuroinflammation. Although its molecular hallmarks are well documented, cell-type-specific mechanisms driving gene dysregulation remain elusive. While single-cell RNA sequencing resolves cellular states, most studies focus on individual genes rather than coordinated programs. Moreover, a gap persists between interpretable network-based models and artificial intelligence foundation models, which capture complex interactions but lack mechanistic transparency. Whether these approaches converge or provide complementary views remains unclear. We present an integrated study combining SCANet, for reconstructing co-expression and gene regulatory networks, with scGPT foundation model. Applied to over 1.3 million cells across 18 cell types, this approach revealed that Alzheimer-associated transcriptional changes concentrate within coherent co-expression modules, for extracellular matrix organization, immune signaling, and neuronal communication. Genes prioritized by scGPT were largely embedded within SCANet modules, indicating convergence at the gene level; however, higher-order architecture agreement was limited and cell-type-specific. Thus, scGPT highlights influential genes, whereas SCANet resolves their modular organization, providing complementary information. By integrating both methods, we recovered known Alzheimer-related pathways and identified novel regulatory candidates, including the CEBPB-CENPQ axis in vulnerable SST-GABA interneurons. This demonstrates that combining network biology with foundation models enables gene prioritization and mechanistic interpretation.

title: A second-generation "hypoxia in a pill" rescues neurodegenerative phenotypes across distinct mouse models.
abstract: A growing body of preclinical research is demonstrating the therapeutic potential of chronic, continuous hypoxia (11% FIO2) for rare and common diseases. However, the chronic delivery of hypoxic gas poses both practical challenges and long-term safety concerns. We previously introduced a small-molecule, "hypoxia-in-a-pill" combining a hemoglobin affinity enhancer (GBT440) to limit oxygen delivery with a HIF-2α inhibitor (PT2399) to prevent detrimental compensatory erythropoiesis. Although this small-molecule regimen extended the lifespan of the Ndufs4 knockout (KO) mouse model of mitochondrial complex I deficiency and Leigh syndrome, its efficacy did not match chronic 11% FIO2. Here we optimize this regimen using GBT601, a second-generation hemoglobin affinity enhancer with longer half-life and greater hemoglobin occupancy, and show it rescues key neurodegenerative phenotypes in multiple models. When we initiate therapy in 50 d old Ndufs4 KO mice with advanced disease, GBT601 monotherapy alleviated neurological disease phenotypes and extended median lifespan from 62 to 105 d, while dual therapy with the GBT601/PT2399 combination extended median lifespan to 158 d. When initiated after onset of advanced disease in a mouse model of Friedreich's ataxia, the combination halted further progression of motor phenotypes. In a mouse model of Parkinson's disease due to α-synuclein toxicity, initiating the GBT601/PT2399 combination after onset of motor dysfunction attenuates brain hyperoxia and lipid peroxidation and reverses motor phenotypes. Importantly, the combination maintained body weight without inducing any signs of pulmonary hypertension. Our findings motivate further preclinical and clinical evaluation of our "hypoxia in a pill" approach for diseases with high unmet need.

title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

title: Metal Oxides Catalyze Formation of Dehydroamino Acids by Phosphate β-Elimination Under Physiological Conditions.
abstract: The dehydroamino acids (DHAAs) dehydroalanine and dehydrobutyrine are formed in proteins posttranslationally from serine and threonine, respectively. They contain an electrophilic alkene, which reacts readily with nucleophiles by Michael addition, giving rise to a variety of chemical modifications as well as protein crosslinks. Recent work has shown DHAAs and their modifications to be highly prevalent in protein aggregates isolated from brains of Alzheimer's Disease (AD) patients. As there is no human enzyme known to catalyze the formation of DHAAs, this raised the question of how they are produced. We show here that metal oxides, particularly the iron oxides goethite and hematite, efficiently catalyze the formation of DHAAs in model phosphopeptides in vitro under physiologically relevant conditions. Iron oxides are known to accumulate in the human brain with age, and this deposition is enhanced in neurodegenerative disorders like AD. The DHAA formation by heterogeneous catalysis reported here provides a previously unknown mechanism linking iron deposition to protein crosslinking in AD and potentially other neurodegenerative diseases where iron accumulation and protein aggregation co-occur.

title: Olive leaf-derived exosome-like vesicles attenuate neurotoxicity in an in vitro rotenone model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease primarily characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and protein aggregation. Despite extensive research, current therapeutic options remain limited to symptomatic management, underscoring the need for neuroprotective strategies targeting disease pathology. In this study, we investigated the neuroprotective potential of exosome-like vesicles derived from olive (Olea europaea) leaves (Ole-ELVs) in an in vitro PD model induced by rotenone in SH-SY5Y human neuroblastoma cells. To evaluate the protective impact of olive leaf-derived ELVs, oxidative stress, cell viability, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation were assessed by measuring reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay, JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential staining, and Thioflavin S staining for α-synuclein aggregation. Our findings indicate that treatment with Ole-ELVs significantly attenuated rotenone-induced ROS production, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduced protein aggregation. Collectively, these results suggest that Ole-ELVs exert neuroprotective effects through antioxidative, protection against cytotoxicity, and mitochondrial-stabilizing mechanisms, offering a promising natural nanoscale therapeutic candidate for PD.

title: Wearable Electromyography and Inertial Sensor Phenotypes Across Clinical Subtypes of Parkinson's Disease.
abstract:
Parkinson's disease (PD) is clinically heterogeneous, yet whether the mild motor-predominant, intermediate, and diffuse malignant (MMP/IM/DM) subtypes show objective neuromuscular and kinematic phenotypic differences remains unclear.
We studied 120 patients with PD (55 men and 65 women) in the medication ON state. Subtypes were assigned using motor, cognitive, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, and autonomic domains. Synchronized surface electromyography and inertial recordings were obtained from the more affected upper limb during three tremor and three movement tasks. Digital motor features were compared across subtypes using covariate-adjusted linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Subject-level associations with DM membership were examined using Firth penalized logistic regression with LASSO-based feature selection.
Of 120 patients, 54 were classified as MMP, 46 as IM, and 20 as DM. Clinical burden showed a graded pattern, with the greatest motor and non-motor impairment in DM. Among all digital motor domains, only amplitude/speed remained significant after FDR correction (p = 0.006). Greater amplitude/speed impairment was associated with DM versus non-DM membership in the Firth logistic regression (OR 2.902, 95% CI 1.201-10.186) and in the subsequent LASSO-selected Firth model (OR 4.444, 95% CI 1.879-13.986). Lower tremor amplitude also independently distinguished DM from non-DM (OR 0.019, 95% CI < 0.001-0.327).
MMP/IM/DM subtypes exhibit measurable EMG/IMU phenotypic differences beyond conventional clinical evaluation. The amplitude/speed domain may represent a candidate digital marker for the DM phenotype, outperforming tremor and other motor domains. Longitudinal and multimodal studies are warranted to validate its prognostic and mechanistic significance.

title: Assessing neuropsychiatric symptoms in context: Integrating standardized and ecological approaches for better care.
abstract: Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are common, disabling, and burdensome core features of dementia that often dominate the disease presentation and trajectory. Despite their prevalence and clinical significance, the assessment of NPS remains challenging in clinical practice. Traditional standardized assessment instruments, while widely used, are limited by their reliance on caregivers' retrospective recall, single time-point measurements, lack of direct observation, and limited ability to capture the NPS dynamic, fluctuating and context-dependent nature. A critical caveat of standardized assessment instruments lies in the insufficient exploration of NPS underlying causes, underscoring the need to refine existing approaches to better assist clinicians in detection, diagnosis, and management.

title: Characteristics of new and re-initiating antiretroviral therapy clients in Malawi: implications for client counseling in resource-constrained settings.
abstract: New antiretroviral treatment (ART) initiates and re-initiators (returning after interruption in treatment [IIT], defined as ≥28 days late for refill) are at higher risk of future IIT compared to stable clients. Counseling is a core strategy to increase retention among new initiates, but little is known about whether re-initiators may have different counseling needs. We compared sociodemographic and psychosocial characteristics of new initiates and re-initiators. We enrolled ART clients ≥15 years living in nine facility catchment areas across three regions of Malawi. We conducted a survey with domains on sociodemographics, ART history, mobility, depression (positive screen: ≥8 on WHO Self-Reporting Questionnaire), and alcohol use (hazardous use: ≥4 for men, ≥3 for women on AUDIT-C). We used Wilcoxon rank-sum and chi-squared tests to assess differences between new initiates and re-initiators. Between September 2023 and April 2025 we screened 1,332 and enrolled 840 eligible ART clients (239 new initiates [28%]). Median age was 38 years; 61% were female. New initiates were more likely than re-initiators to be younger (33 vs. 39 years, p < 0.01), pregnant (21% vs. 4%, p < 0.01), unaware of spouse's HIV status (63% vs. 4%, p < 0.01), screened positive for depression (48% vs. 26%, p < 0.01), and reporting high-risk alcohol usage (34% vs. 19%, p = 0.03). New initiates were less likely to be mobile (21% traveled ≥30 nights in last 12 months vs. 60%, p < 0.01). Counseling should address different needs for new vs. re-initiating clients, targeting depression, alcohol use and disclosure among all clients, disclosure and DSD models for new initiates, and mobility for re-initiators.

title: Rapid Qualitative Analysis to Inform Preimplementation of a Stepped-Care Model for Depression Care Among Older People Living With HIV in Ibadan, Nigeria.
abstract:
Depression is common among older adults living with HIV (OLHIV) and is associated with poor antiretroviral adherence and higher viral load. Despite the importance of addressing psychological health issues in older people living with HIV, there is a paucity of tailored depression interventions for low-resource settings. Although the stepped-care task-sharing (SCT) intervention model is effective for depression in low-resource settings, it has not been applied to this population. This study examined preimplementation requirements for piloting a SCT model for depression among OLHIV in a government-funded clinic in Southwest Nigeria.
We conducted a qualitative preimplementation study, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), to assess the contextual fit and feasibility of integrating a SCT intervention for depression into routine HIV services. In-depth interviews were conducted with healthcare providers and older adults with HIV at the Infectious Disease Institute, Ibadan, Nigeria. Data were analyzed using rapid qualitative methods to identify CFIR-informed barriers, facilitators, and adaptation needs to guide intervention refinement prior to pilot testing.
Twenty-two interviews were conducted with healthcare providers (n = 11) and OLHIV (n = 11), each lasting 30-45 min. Findings indicated that the SCT intervention was perceived as feasible, supported by staff willingness and existing clinic structures that could be leveraged during pilot testing. Key barriers to implementation included high workload, limited provider training, stigma, discontinuity of care, and financial constraints. Facilitators included organizational readiness and high acceptability among service users.
The SCT model is perceived as acceptable and potentially feasible for integrating depression care into HIV services for OLHIV. However, it requires adaptation into existing workflows, provider capacity, and patient follow-up routines. Findings provide insights to refine the intervention processes in preparation for pilot testing and integration of psychological healthcare into HIV services.

title: Multilevel Barriers and Facilitators to HIV Care Engagement Among Virally Unsuppressed People Living With HIV in the U.S. Deep South: A Qualitative Study.
abstract: The U.S. South experiences disproportionate HIV-related morbidity and persistently lower viral suppression rates. Achieving Ending the HIV Epidemic goals requires understanding multilevel influences on care engagement among virally unsuppressed people living with HIV. We conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with 30 virally unsuppressed people living with HIV receiving care across Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi. Guided by the Modified Social Ecological Model, we examined individual, interpersonal, clinic, community, and policy-level factors shaping engagement and antiretroviral therapy adherence. Participants described intersecting structural and psychosocial barriers, including financial insecurity, transportation challenges, depression, and internalized stigma. Social networks functioned as both support and stigma, particularly within family and faith contexts. Clinics served as critical anchors when providing confidential, holistic services addressing social needs, although inefficiencies and resource constraints disrupted continuity. Persistent discrimination, restrictive policies, funding instability, and HIV criminalization further threatened engagement, underscoring the need for multilevel interventions to improve viral suppression.

title: The Wnt5a-PKCδ-GluA1 axis controls synapse-specific plasticity in HIV-1 gp120-induced pain pathogenesis.
abstract: Imbalance of excitatory and inhibitory neuronal activity (E/I imbalance) plays a critical role in pain pathogenesis. Recent studies have identified a novel form of E/I imbalance in the spinal dorsal horn of animal models of HIV-associated pain, manifesting as increased spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic current (sEPSC) frequency in excitatory neurons alongside decreased sEPSC frequency in inhibitory neurons and hence termed neural circuitry polarization. However, how the opposite forms of synaptic plasticity in neural circuitry polarization are coordinated in the pain neural circuit is unclear. Here, we show that in the spinal dorsal horn of a mouse model of HIV-associated pain, potentiation of excitatory synapses on excitatory neurons (ESE) and depression of excitatory synapses on inhibitory neurons (ESI) employ distinct mechanisms to support their expression. We found the increase of sEPSC frequency in excitatory neurons induced by HIV-1 gp120 was mediated by a postsynaptic mechanism, whereas decrease of sEPSC frequency in inhibitory neurons was mediated by a presynaptic mechanism. Our studies showed that pharmacological inhibition of calcium-permeable AMPA (CP-AMPA) receptors selectively attenuated potentiation of ESE without significantly affecting ESI depression. We also observed that GluA1 was upregulated in excitatory but not inhibitory neurons, indicating selective CP-AMPA receptor formation in excitatory neurons. Furthermore, we identified a new pain-related signalling pathway in ESE: Wnt5a-PKCδ-GluA1. We elucidated that the GluA1 upregulation and ESE potentiation were controlled by neuronal Wnt5a signalling via protein kinase C delta (PKCδ). Our findings reveal that ESE and ESI in the spinal dorsal horn of HIV pain models use distinct synaptic and molecular mechanisms to support their expression in neural circuitry polarization, demonstrating specialized regulatory pathways for the plasticity of excitatory synapses targeting different neuron types during the pain pathogenesis.

title: Beyond WEIRD populations: Interpreting the gap between subjective cognitive complaints and objective impairment.
abstract: Subjective cognitive complaints (SCC) are shifting from a quasi-diagnostic marker to a multidimensional clinical signal. Leniz et al. use the semi-rural Chilean MAUCO cohort to extend this debate beyond Western-dominated settings. They show a subjective-objective discrepancy: baseline objective performance did not predict incident SCC, whereas benzodiazepine use, and depressive symptoms did, highlighting affective and iatrogenic influences. Yet SCC predicted incident cognitive impairment. We argue that these findings are better interpreted by a model of SCC with at least two-components: affective/iatrogenic and degeneration-related components. In resource-limited contexts, SCC may aid risk-enrichment while prompting medication and mood review.

title: Cognitive predictors of functioning and treatment response in treatment-resistant psychosis: A transdiagnostic approach.
abstract:
Patients with primary psychotic disorders who fail to respond adequately to standard antipsychotic treatments are defined as treatment-resistant. While neuropsychological assessment is crucial for evaluating cognitive impairment, its utility in predicting functional and treatment outcomes in individuals with treatment-resistant psychosis (TRP) remains understudied. This study investigates whether neuropsychological functioning predicts functional and treatment outcomes in TRP, utilizing a transdiagnostic approach.
An archival retrospective chart review study was conducted on inpatients who received neuropsychological evaluations within the British Columbia Psychosis Program, utilizing neuropsychological, clinical outcome, as well as functional performance and capacity data. Principal component regression was applied to the neuropsychological test battery to determine the association between cognitive factors and functional and treatment outcomes.
Neuropsychological assessment of the inpatients (N = 206) revealed difficulties in processing speed, working memory, and executive function, and deficits in verbal and nonverbal memory. Principal component analysis identified four cognitive domains: Executive Function/Processing Speed, Crystallized Cognitive Abilities, Visuospatial Ability, and Verbal Memory and Learning. After controlling for symptom severity, Crystallized Cognitive Abilities (B = 0.939, SE = 0.429, p = .030) and Verbal Memory and Learning (B = 0.891, SE = 0.426, p = .038) modestly predicted functional performance, but no associations emerged for functional capacity or treatment outcomes.
These findings highlight the complex relationship between cognition, daily functioning, and treatment outcomes in TRP. This study stresses the importance of a transdiagnostic approach and advocates further research into mediators of cognition-functioning relationships to improve understanding and interventions for TRP.

title: Tobacco use moderates associations between cannabis use, psychiatric symptoms, and cognitive performance in psychosis spectrum disorders.
abstract: Tobacco and cannabis use are highly prevalent among individuals with psychotic disorders. Tobacco use has been consistently linked to poorer clinical and cognitive outcomes, whereas findings regarding cannabis use remain mixed. The present study was a secondary analysis of cross-sectional data from the Bipolar-Schizophrenia Network on Intermediate Phenotypes 2, a large multi-site psychosis spectrum sample with cognitive and clinical assessments. The primary aim was to more precisely characterize how tobacco or cannabis use, co-use, and non-use differentially relate to clinical and cognitive function. The final sample included 884 individuals with psychotic disorders without diagnosis of substance abuse in the past 30 days or substance dependence in the past 3 months for any substance except tobacco. Among individuals with psychosis, tobacco-only users demonstrated greater symptom burden and worse cognitive impairment than several comparison psychosis substance groups. In contrast, cannabis use showed more nuanced associations. Greater adult cannabis use was tied to worse general psychopathology for current tobacco users but fewer general symptoms among those who never used tobacco. More adult cannabis use was linked to better cognitive performance for current tobacco users but was not linked to working memory among past tobacco users. These findings highlight tobacco use as a potential marker of greater disease severity and cognitive impairment among individuals with psychosis, while also demonstrating the importance of considering patterns of co-occurring use of substances.

title: Neurocognition and social cognition as risk markers in adolescents: a comparative study of asymptomatic siblings of Early-Onset Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
abstract: Early-Onset Schizophrenia (EOS) and Early-Onset Bipolar Disorder (EOBD) share overlapping clinical and genetic features. This study aims to compare the neuro-social cognitive performance of healthy siblings of adolescents with EOS (EOS-Sib) and EOBD (EOBD-Sib) to identify candidate neurocognitive markers of familial liability and evaluate the impact of environmental stressors, such as childhood trauma, on neurocognitive and social cognitive performance. The study included 164 participants: 36 EOS-Sib, 40 EOBD-Sib, and 88 healthy controls (HC) aged 11-23. All subjects underwent a rigorous screening process using the semi structured interview (K-SADS-PL) to exclude any psychopathology. Neuro-social cognitive performance was assessed using the University of Pennsylvania Computerized Neurocognitive Battery. Also, Childhood Trauma Questionnaire and Children's Depression Rating Scale are used for the clinical evaluation. A composite 'G-score' was derived to represent global neurocognitive performance. Although both sibling groups differed from healthy controls on selected neurocognitive measures, no significant differences were detected between the EOS-Sib and EOBD-Sib groups, indicating substantial overlap in neurocognitive performance across the two familial-risk groups. This null finding suggests shared transdiagnostic neurocognitive vulnerability rather than disorder-specific cognitive differentiation at the familial-risk level. After controlling for age, maternal education, paternal education, depressive symptom severity, and childhood trauma, both EOS-Sib and EOBD-Sib groups exhibited significant deficits in global neurocognitive performance compared to healthy controls (p < .001). For emotion recognition (ER), a significant impairment was observed only in the EOS-Sib group (p = .003). Childhood trauma was independently associated with poorer ER performance (p = .007), but was not significantly associated with general neurocognitive performance (p = .746). The Neurocognitive G-score demonstrated good group-level discriminative ability between adolescents with familial liability and healthy controls (AUC = 0.805). In conclusion, unaffected siblings of adolescents with EOS and EOBD exhibited overlapping neurocognitive impairments, particularly in executive functioning and working memory, supporting these domains as candidate neurocognitive markers associated with familial liability. The Neurocognitive G-score demonstrated good group-level discriminative ability between adolescents with known familial liability and healthy controls; however, it should be regarded as an exploratory neurocognitive risk indicator rather than a definitive screening tool, and longitudinal studies are needed to determine its prognostic value for future psychopathology. Furthermore, childhood trauma was independently associated with poorer ER performance after adjustment for relevant covariates, highlighting the potential contribution of environmental adversity to social cognitive functioning in at-risk adolescents.

title: Plasma interleukin-6 levels and treatment responses to antipsychotics in schizophrenia: Focus on clozapine treatment.
abstract: Neuroinflammation is a key pathophysiological mechanism underlying treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS). Interleukin (IL)-6 is a trait-related biomarker that exhibits consistently elevated levels in schizophrenia. However, studies focusing on TRS and examining the associations of clozapine treatment with inflammatory marker and clinical characteristics remain limited. Therefore, this multicenter cross-sectional study focused on patients with TRS and antipsychotic-responsive schizophrenia (ARS). Plasma IL-6 levels were measured in all participants, while plasma clozapine and N-desmethylclozapine concentrations were quantified in patients with TRS. Psychotic symptoms and cognitive function were assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) and the Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia-Short Form (BAC-SF), respectively. Multiple regression analysis was conducted to identify clinical factors associated with plasma IL-6 levels in the TRS group. In total, 37 patients with TRS and 22 with ARS were included in this study. Plasma IL-6 levels were significantly higher in the TRS group than in the ARS group (p < 0.001). In the TRS group, clozapine treatment duration was negatively associated with plasma IL-6 levels after adjustment for age, diabetes mellitus, and treatment setting (β = -0.398; p = 0.031). No significant associations were observed between plasma IL-6 levels and psychiatric symptom severity (PANSS total) or cognitive function (BAC-SF) in the TRS group. Overall, these findings suggest that TRS may differ from ARS in terms of peripheral inflammatory profiles and that longer-term clozapine treatment may be associated with lower plasma IL-6 levels in TRS.

title: The Relationship of Peripheral Glycoprotein Nonmetastatic Melanoma Protein B and Parkinson's Disease: Insights From a Mendelian Randomization Study.
abstract:
Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have revealed that glycoprotein nonmetastatic melanoma Protein B (GPNMB) was associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). GPNMB has been found in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, and its levels and the variation of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) have been linked to disease severity in PD patients. However, whether the altered expression of GPNMB is the cause or the result cannot be identified in the patient samples.
This study applied a Mendelian randomization analysis to explore the causal relationship between GPNMB and PD. The blood GPNMB mRNA level from the expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) dataset and the plasma GPNMB protein level from the protein quantitative trait loci (pQTL) acted as the exposure. PD's GWAS dataset from the International Parkinson's Disease Genomics Consortium including 33674 PD cases and 449056 normal controls was applied as the outcome.
MR analysis with the inverse-variant weighted method (IVW, OR = 1.416, p = 1.39e - 06) and the weighted median methods (WM, OR = 1.430, p = 4.47e - 07) showed that the plasma GPNMB protein expression was linked to a higher risk of PD. We also discovered a significant association between the blood mRNA level of GPNMB and PD risk. The IVW (OR = 1.243, p = 3.64e - 09) and WM (OR = 1.237, p = 5.11e - 08) methods share similar results. Secondary MR analysis further reveals causality between GPNMB pQTL/eQTL and brain volume traits.
The study demonstrated a significant association between plasma GPNMB protein (pQTL) and mRNA level (eQTL) with PD. Further secondary MR analysis revealed causality between GPNMB pQTL/eQTL and brain volume traits.

title: Modulation of odorant-binding protein fibrillogenesis in crowded environments.
abstract: Amyloid aggregation of proteins with β-barrel topology is increasingly being considered in relation to pathological processes in humans. Nevertheless, the influence of the densely packed intracellular and extracellular environments (macromolecular crowding conditions) on the fibrillogenesis of these highly structured proteins remains insufficiently studied. Addressing this gap, we focused our analysis on odorant-binding proteins (OBPs), as recent studies suggest the involvement of their amyloidogenesis in olfactory dysfunction, particularly in neurodegenerative diseases. Within the bovine OBP (bOBP) model, a stage-specific and polymer-dependent effect of crowding conditions on β-barrel protein fibrillogenesis was demonstrated using various crowding agents, polyethylene glycol (PEG-8k and PEG-12k) and dextran (Dex-15-25k and Dex-70k), and a comprehensive range of physicochemical methods. Specifically, the addition of PEGs shortened and even eliminated the lag phase of fibrillogenesis by accelerating primary nucleation. Concurrently, all crowding agents attenuated the processes of the exponential phase of fibrillogenesis. These effects of crowding agents were attributed to: 1) inhibition of global structural transformations in the β-barrel, and 2) enhanced clustering of formed aggregates, which suppresses secondary processes like fibril fragmentation. The combined action of crowding agents reduced mature amyloid formation, promoted the accumulation of highly hydrophobic and cytotoxic prefibrillar precursors, and generated clusters of structurally heterogeneous aggregates. Our findings reveal that macromolecular crowding influences the fibrillogenesis trajectory and the properties of amyloid aggregates formed from β-barrel proteins, which must be considered when analyzing the biological consequences of these processes in vivo.

title: Cognitive performance and self-reported physical exercise in bipolar disorder: A cross-sectional analysis of pre-randomization screening data from an ongoing randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
Bipolar Disorder (BD) is frequently associated with persistent cognitive deficits that significantly impair functionality and quality of life. While physical exercise (PE) has shown promise in improving cognition in healthy individuals and those with other psychiatric conditions, most consistently in major depressive disorder and schizophrenia, its specific impact on individuals with BD remains under-investigated. This study aimed to investigate the association between self-reported regular physical exercise and cognitive performance in individuals with Bipolar Disorder.
This study consists of a cross-sectional analysis of pre-randomization screening data from an ongoing randomized controlled trial. The analysis included 108 euthymic BD individuals (aged 18-55) recruited from the outpatient clinic at the University of São Paulo Medical School (PROMAN). Participants were allocated into either the Exercise Group (n = 48), defined by self-reported engagement in regular structured physical exercise at least twice a week, and the No-Exercise Group (n = 60); exercise status was ascertained with a brief in-house checklist. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Screen for Cognitive Impairment in Psychiatry (SCIP). Secondary measures included mood symptoms (MADRS and YMRS) and pharmacological treatment profiles. Effect sizes were estimated with Cohen's d, and a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of α = 0.0033 was applied to the 15 comparisons performed.
The Exercise group demonstrated significantly higher SCIP Total Scores compared to the No-Exercise group (64.63 ± 9.19 vs. 56.50 ± 7.84; p < 0.001, d = 0.95). Significant advantages for the exercise group were observed in sub-domains related to verbal learning (p = 0.010) and working memory (p = 0.002); the total score and working memory remained significant after Bonferroni correction, whereas verbal learning did not. Notably, the No-Exercise group had a significantly higher usage of stimulants (27.5% vs. 4.5%, p = 0.029), while the Exercise group had a higher prevalence of anticonvulsant use (45.5% vs. 20%, p = 0.035); neither medication difference survived correction.
Exercise status was self-reported and dichotomous, with no data on intensity, duration or modality, and no demographic or clinical covariates were available for adjustment.
Regular physical exercise appears to be associated with superior global cognition, verbal learning, and working memory in individuals with BD. These findings, derived from the screening phase of an ongoing trial, suggest that PE may be a promising adjunctive strategy for neurocognitive rehabilitation, although the cross-sectional design precludes any causal inference.

title: Nanopore sequencing combined with adaptive sampling and NanoExpansion enables accurate characterization of repeat expansion disorders.
abstract: Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1, n = 51) and DM2 (n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington's disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and 4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington's disease, and Kennedy disease cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, long-PCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington's disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate, comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

title: Partial convergence of alternative polyadenylation changes across ALS-Associated RNA-Binding proteins.
abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) regulates transcript 3'-end architecture, stability, localization, and translation. Although RNA-binding protein dysfunction is central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), whether different ALS-associated proteins cause shared APA abnormalities remains unclear. We analyzed poly(A)-site usage after TDP-43 knockdown, TDP-43 K263E expression, FUS knockout, FUS P525L expression, and MATR3 knockout. Using false-discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 as the primary criterion, evidence varied markedly among datasets. FUS knockout produced the strongest response, with 373 significant events affecting 239 genes. Three events involving two genes remained significant after TDP-43 knockdown, and two events involving one gene remained significant in the TDP-43 K263E dataset. No events survived FDR correction after FUS P525L expression or MATR3 knockout, and no FDR-significant events or genes were shared between datasets. We therefore examined nominal events (unadjusted P < 0.05) as an explicitly exploratory layer. Nominal event overlap was enriched in 7 of 10 pairwise comparisons, and nominal gene overlap in 9 of 10. TDP-43 knockdown and TDP-43 K263E showed the strongest directional agreement: 65 nominal events were shared; 25 were directionally classified in both datasets, of which 23 were concordant. FUS knockout and FUS P525L also showed enriched nominal overlap, but without significant directional concordance or correlated ΔPAU responses. Thus, FUS loss induces a robust FDR-supported APA phenotype, whereas evidence is substantially weaker in other contexts. Cross-dataset similarities occur mainly among exploratory nominal targets and do not consistently extend to direction or magnitude. APA responses therefore show partial, context-dependent convergence rather than a universal defect.

title: Tryptophan metabolomic profiling in persons with and without HIV.
abstract:
Full tryptophan (T) profiling allows determination of T-metabolites from the serotonin, kynurenine (K) and gut-integrity/indole pathways. We assessed T-metabolites, depressive symptoms, cognitive function and sleep measures in persons with and without HIV.
Persons with HIV on ART and lifestyle-similar persons without HIV completed depressive symptoms questionnaire (PHQ-9), cognitive testing (T-score), actigraphy sleep measures and early morning fasting blood sampling for metabolomic profiling (LC-MS, UK National Phenome Centre). Statistical analysis used Mann-Whitney U tests and Spearman rank correlation.
Of 468 individuals (345 with HIV), 81% were male individuals and median age was 58 (IQR 53-63) years. Several metabolites, including K, K/T ratio, citrulline and 5-hydroxyindole-acetic-acid, differed in those with and without HIV. Median (IQR) PHQ-9 scores were 5 (1-10) and 1 (0-3) in those with and without HIV, respectively. In those with HIV, higher PHQ-9 scores were associated with higher K-pathway markers [quinolinic acid (P = 0.05), K (P = 0.02) and K/T ratio (P = 0.02)] but associations were generally weaker in those without HIV. Cognitive testing T-score [with HIV: 50 (44-54.9); without HIV: 52 (48.3-55.8)] was positively associated with higher gut-integrity/indole-markers in those with HIV [citrulline (P < 0.0001), indole-3-acetic-acid (P < 0.0001)], but less so in those without HIV. No associations between any actigraphy sleep measures and T-metabolites were observed.
K-pathway metabolites (driven by peripheral inflammatory responses) are associated with depressive symptoms and metabolites of gut health associated with cognitive function in those with HIV; these observations were less evident in those without HIV. Further understanding of these mechanisms could assist the development of future therapeutic interventions.

title: Age-associated differences in mentalizing error profiles in schizophrenia: Evidence for a dissociation between hypo- and hyper-mentalizing.
abstract:
Theory of mind (ToM) impairments are a core feature of schizophrenia and are strongly associated with functional outcomes. However, ToM is often treated as a unitary construct, potentially obscuring distinct patterns of mentalizing errors. This study examined whether age is differentially associated with hyper- and hypo-mentalizing in schizophrenia.
ToM was assessed in 177 individuals with schizophrenia and 142 healthy controls using the Movie for the Assessment of Social Cognition (MASC). Generalized linear models examined age, diagnosis, and their interaction on total ToM errors, hyper-mentalizing, hypo-mentalizing, and the hypo-hyper error ratio. Schizophrenia-only models adjusted for sex, verbal IQ, positive and negative symptoms, illness duration, and medication use. A sensitivity analysis in 156 individuals with schizophrenia with available verbal-memory data additionally adjusted for verbal memory.
In case-control analyses, older age was associated with greater total ToM and hypo-mentalizing errors, with a stronger age-hypo-mentalizing association in schizophrenia. In schizophrenia-only analyses, age was associated with greater total ToM errors, hypo-mentalizing, and a higher hypo-hyper error ratio. Hyper-mentalizing was associated with positive symptoms and verbal IQ, but not age. In the sensitivity analysis, age remained significantly associated only with hypo-mentalizing; hyper-mentalizing remained associated with positive symptoms. No robust nonlinear age effects were observed.
Cross-sectional age differences in schizophrenia are characterized by a selective association between older age and hypo-mentalizing, whereas hyper-mentalizing shows a distinct pattern of cognitive and symptom-related correlates. These findings suggest that age is differentially associated with mentalizing error types in schizophrenia, with a selective association with hypo-mentalizing.

title: Multidimensional Cognitive and Linguistic Profiles in Adolescent Schizo-Obsessive Presentations: A Machine Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence Approach.
abstract: Schizo-obsessive presentations in adolescence remain insufficiently characterized, particularly with respect to their cognitive, linguistic, and social-cognitive features. This study explored clinical, neurocognitive, social-cognitive, and thought-language characteristics associated with schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and schizo-obsessive presentations in adolescents using a Support Vector Machine-based explainable machine learning framework. A total of 182 adolescents were included: schizophrenia with comorbid OCD (n = 27), schizophrenia without obsessive-compulsive symptoms (n = 55), and OCD without psychotic symptoms (n = 100). The model demonstrated high discriminative performance overall, although classification performance was lower for the schizo-obsessive group, suggesting partial overlap with both schizophrenia and OCD presentations. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses indicated that obsessive-compulsive symptom burden and negative symptom burden were the primary dimensions associated with classification, while social cognition, verbal fluency, verbal memory, executive functioning, processing speed, thought-language organization, and prosodic features also contributed to group differentiation. The findings suggest that schizo-obsessive presentations may involve broader cognitive and linguistic characteristics beyond symptom-level overlap and support a multidimensional approach to their clinical evaluation.

title: Synaptic plasticity of prefrontal long-range inhibition regulates cognitive flexibility.
abstract: While glutamatergic synaptic plasticity is believed to be a fundamental mechanism mediating learning, the behavioral significance of plasticity at cortical GABAergic synapses remains less well understood. Furthermore, despite recent discoveries of long-range projections from neocortical GABAergic neurons, details about how they function are also sparse. Here, we combine behavioral optogenetics with patch-clamp electrophysiology to link plasticity at long-range GABAergic synapses with higher-order cognitive functions. Specifically, learning extradimensional rule shifts potentiates callosal GABAergic synapses from prefrontal parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons onto corticothalamic neurons. Disrupting this potentiation by inhibiting callosal PV terminals during rule shifts induces perseveration, whereas reinstating this potentiation with subsequent gamma-frequency callosal PV terminal stimulation restores flexible behavior. This shows how a novel plasticity locus can regulate brain circuits underlying normal cognition and pathological states.
